newsitem.title: JAPAN: Nomura's top ranking seen surviving scandal.
newsitem.headline: Nomura's top ranking seen surviving scandal.

text.p: A scandal over suspected illegal deals and possible payoffs to a one-time racketeer will hit Nomura Securities profits as well as its pride.
But analysts say the giant brokerage is unlikely to lose its top ranking in Japan's securities industry.

"They're pretty well top across the board, and I find it hard to imagine that they could slip to number two across a large number of product lines for an extended period of time," said Walter Altherr, senior financial analyst at Jardine Fleming Securities.

Two Nomura directors resigned on Monday after the brokerage firm said they made apparently illegal deals and funnelled funds to a corporate client which has linked by Japanese media to a former "sokaiya" racketeer.
Company president Hideo Sakamaki is also expected to step down over the scandal, possibly this month.

The latest blow to Nomura's public image comes six years after top executives Setsuya Tabuchi and Yoshihisa Tabuchi (no relation) resigned over revelations the brokerage had compensated favoured clients for losses and that affiliates had dealt with gangsters.

Major Japanese asset management firms including Nomura's own unit, Nomura Investment Management Co, said on Monday that they had suspended business with Nomura Securities after the brokerage revealed the suspected illegal deals.
Most firms said they would wait for the results of a probe by the Securities and Exchange Surveillance Commission (SESC) before resuming business with the scandal-tainted brokerage.
Concerns are also surfacing that the fresh incident might affect Nomura's important underwriting business.
A Tokyo Metropolitan Government official denied a newspaper report that Tokyo had basically decided to exclude Nomura from its underwriting syndicate as early as next month.
But he told Reuters that the city would be watching the results of the SESC investigation.
"The business at risk is potentially 50 percent of new revenues, between commissions and underwriting," said James Fiorillo, financial analyst at ING Baring Securities.
"Profitability is still of paramount importance and when you get fined and lose face, it's a major problem," he added.
Some analysts said they would be watching the fate of the two Tabuchis, who rejoined Nomura's board in 1995, for clues to how serious the brokerage was about internal reform.

"You've got an organisation that was basically built up by Tabuchi et Tabuchi and most of the people in senior positions are indebted to and supported by them," said David Threadgold, analyst at BZW Securities.
"Symbolic resignations are fairly easy but what do they do after that, and will the resignations include the Tabuchis?"
Also unclear is how stiff the official penalties will be.
Finance Minister Hiroshi Mitsuzuka said on Tuesday that the ministry would decide what steps to take after hearing from the SESC, but hinted the measures might be stern.

The finance minister could, depending on the SESC findings, revoke Nomura's licenses or order it to halt some or all business for up to six months. Should the deals be found to have violated the Commercial Code's ban on payoffs to "sokaiya" racketeers, legal action could also be initiated.
Sokaiya extort money from a company by threatening to disrupt shareholders' meetings.
Analysts said, however, that the heaviest possible penalties were unlikely to be imposed.
"It's not in the best interests of the authorities to cripple Nomura, although they want to be seen as making them pay for it," Fiorillo said.
Many investors are probably keen to return to Nomura as soon as possible given the brokerage's overwhelming strength in key areas such as distribution, research and product knowledge.

"Every fund manager ultimately wants to outperform the market and if they believe dealing with Nomura will help them to do that, in the long-run and maybe in the short-run they will find a way to restore these relationships," Altherr said.
Others agreed Nomura would likely retain its Number One position in the domestic brokerage industry, although its share of some markets might slip temporarily.
"Nomura dominates so much...if you're going to be in the Japanese market, to an extent, you have to deal with them," said Robert Garone, analyst at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson International.
